If some of your favourite video games were actually tech demos for completely different games? In this episode of Fact Hunt, Guru Larry uncovers the bizarre video game tech demos, prototype games and secret development projects that helped create some of gaming's biggest titles.

From The Bouncer and Final Fantasy to War Gods and Mortal Kombat 4, Motor Toon Grand Prix and Gran Turismo, Rockstar Games Presents Table Tennis and Grand Theft Auto IV, and Pilotwings 64 and Super Mario 64 — these seemingly unrelated games were used to experiment with new hardware, graphics, physics and technology.

Some were disguised experiments. Some were stepping stones towards much bigger games. And some were simply bizarre ways for developers to test what their new hardware could actually do!

In this episode we look at the hidden history of video games, retro gaming technology, PlayStation 2, PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Xbox 360, game engines, physics technology and the strange development stories behind some of the most famous games ever made.

So how did a cartoon kart racer help lead to Gran Turismo? Why did Rockstar make a table tennis game before GTA IV? And what did a bizarre 3D fighting game have to do with Mortal Kombat 4?

Find out in Fact Hunt: Games That Were Tech Demos for Other Games!

And yes, before you ask, I'm "That Guru Larry" that was on TV 😂

Why is Bubsy 3D universally considered one of the worst video games ever made? In this retro gaming retrospective, we break down the infamous history of the Bubsy series—from its Sonic-inspired 2D side-scrollers with frustrating one-hit deaths to the ultimate disaster on the original PlayStation.

We take a deep dive into the legendary 93% Gold X Award review from PSExtreme that rated Bubsy 3D on par with PS1 classics like Tekken, Twisted Metal, and DOOM. Plus, we cover developer Eidetic’s rebound into Syphon Filter and Bend Studio, as well as Bubsy’s modern revivals like The Woolies Strike Back, Paws of Fire, Limited Run's Bubsy 3D remaster, and Atari's Bubsy 4D!

Did you know that Pixar once took Nintendo and the creators of Grand Theft Auto to court over a sentient unicycle?

Back in 1994, DMA Design (now known as Rockstar North) developed a blazing-fast, 16-bit platform racer for the Super Nintendo called Uniracers (known as Unirally in PAL regions). Featuring innovative physics and roller-coaster tracks, it seemed like a surefire hit. But there was just one problem: Pixar—fresh off their early computer-animated shorts—felt the game's animated unicycle looked and moved just a bit too much like Red from their 1987 short film Red’s Dream.

What followed was one of the strangest, most fascinating copyright battles in entertainment history, ultimately resulting in a court victory for Pixar, a cancelled Japanese release, and a rare collector's item that remains trapped in legal limbo to this day.

Game Over screens are meant to stop you in your tracks, but sometimes game designers decided to go completely off the rails and make failure bizarre, hilarious, and strangely brutal. In this episode of Fact Hunt, Guru Larry takes a look at some of the most ridiculous, confusing, and unexpectedly dark Game Overs ever put into video games — from planet-destroying curiosity in Commander Keen, to spine-snapping forbidden knowledge in Alone in the Dark, to the bizarrely tragic ending of The New Zealand Story, the unfair nonsense of Return to Zork, and the shockingly grim punishment lurking in California Games 2.

So buckle up for a trip through the daftest defeats, the laughable losses, and the most unhinged ways a game has ever told you that you have failed. If you enjoy retro gaming oddities, dark humour, and the sort of trivia that makes game designers look mildly unwell, you are in the right place.

Special thanks to @DeuteriumtheSentientMattress for helping write and edit today's episode!

In 2020, Ubisoft launched Immortals Fenyx Rising — a brand-new mythology adventure from the makers of Assassin's Creed Odyssey that seemed to appear out of nowhere. 
However, behind the colourful world and awkwardly memorable title lies a far stranger story involving cancelled plans, legal headaches, and a mysterious identity change from a game Ubisoft had already revealed to the world.

In this video, Guru Larry uncovers the bizarre behind-the-scenes drama surrounding the game, the unexpected forces that shaped its fate, and how one of Ubisoft’s most unusual releases became caught up in a battle far bigger than the game itself, ultimately leading to it bombing.

And yes, before you ask, I'm "That Guru Larry" that was on TV 😂

From broken AI in Aliens: Colonial Marines, to game-breaking bugs in Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour, to chat exploits that could literally crash your console in Tony Hawk’s Underground 2—these are the issues developers left behind.
